title: Why Less is More (Sometimes): A Theory of Data Curation
one_liner: A theory that predicts when training on carefully selected hard or easy examples beats training on all data.
lead: A new paradox has shattered the old rule that more data is always better, because a sprawling dataset wastes training on examples the model already understands. Recent machine learning methods train models on tiny curated datasets and achieve better accuracy than methods using full datasets, because they keep only hard, correct examples and discard easy noise. This paper builds a mathematical theory to predict exactly when less data wins, based on how good your labeler and your data-picker are.

paras: For decades, the rule was simple: collect more data, get better models, because each example shrank the error a little. Bigger datasets meant higher accuracy, because you had more chances to learn. But in the last year, researchers discovered something strange: pick the right 100,000 examples from a dataset of 1.2 million, and you beat a model trained on all 1.2 million, because the extra 1.1 million examples were mostly noise that confused training. This contradicts everything we thought we knew about learning.

A beginner would assume you always want all the data you can get. But that misses a key fact: not all examples teach the model equally. Some examples are so easy the model already knows how to handle them and wastes training steps on them. Some are so weird or mislabeled that they point training in the wrong direction. A tiny gold-plated set of truly hard, truly correct examples can teach faster than a sprawling noisy mess, because every training step counts.

callout.html: The paper shows that under certain conditions, a model trained on a small curated subset outperforms a model trained on the full dataset, because when your labeler and picker are aligned with truth, hard examples pack more learning signal per step than the diluted mix of all examples.

panels.title: 5. The payoff
panels.caption: Smaller curated dataset reaches higher accuracy with less wasted learning.

steps.text: Decide what your pruner (the thing picking examples) can see: only features? features and labels?
Compute how closely your labeler, your picker, and ground truth agree on what each example is.
Use the alignment scores to calculate: at what dataset size does keep-hard beat keep-all?
If alignment is high, keep hard examples. If alignment is low, keep easy examples to avoid noisy mistakes.
Train the model on the curated set and check that theory's prediction matches real accuracy.

paras: The paper changes which examples stay in your training set and which get thrown away. Instead of keeping all n examples equally, it keeps some and discards others based on a pruning rule (a rule that decides if an example is worth learning from).

hidden.name: Alignment between labeler, picker, and truth
paras: The paper measures a hidden quantity called alignment: how closely do three things agree? (1) The labeler (the person or oracle that assigns correct labels to training data). (2) The picker (the oracle that selects which examples to keep). (3) Ground truth (what is actually correct). If all three agree perfectly, alignment is high. If the labeler is sloppy or the picker is blind, alignment is low.

The paper estimates alignment from the training data by computing four constants (rho, rho-star, beta, beta-tilde) that capture geometric relationships between these three. These numbers then predict which curation strategy (keep-hard or keep-easy) minimizes test error.

heat.caption: Darker means higher alignment or better curation. When top rows are dark (high agreement), keep-hard wins; when bottom rows are dark (curated), accuracy improves.

reads.html: Alignment is the degree to which your labeler and your picker both point to ground truth. High alignment means they agree; low alignment means they are guessing. This alignment predicts whether keeping hard examples beats keeping all examples.

The paper formalizes alignment via constants rho (generator-truth correlation), rho-star (pruner-truth correlation), beta (oracle loss curvature), and beta-tilde (pruned loss curvature). These are derived from random matrix theory (a branch of math that studies large tables of numbers and their properties), and their relative magnitudes determine the optimal curation strategy.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: the alignment decides everything
paras: The paper's mechanism is stark and simple. Train a model on n examples where all are weighted equally (standard training). Now imagine a pruner that can either keep only hard examples or only easy ones. Which is better depends entirely on whether your labels are trustworthy, because trustworthy labels let you identify real hard examples worth learning from.

It depends entirely on alignment. If your labeler is excellent (correctly labels all training data) and your picker is excellent (can reliably tell hard from easy), then keep-hard is optimal: hard examples pack the most learning per example because they lie at the boundary where the model makes mistakes. Each hard example forces the model to improve because training pulls hardest on examples that are currently wrong, and hard examples are wrong more often. Easy examples waste time repeating what the model already knows. By throwing away easy examples, you double down on signal and cut noise.

But if your labeler is poor (noisy or self-generated from an earlier weak model), the picker becomes unreliable because its decisions are built on faulty labels. In this scenario, hard examples from noisy training often contain mislabeled or contradictory data. Keeping easy examples protects you: they are more likely to be correct, even from a weak labeler, because the labeler's errors are random noise, and easy examples tolerate noise better. This is critical for mitigating model collapse, where a model trained on its own flawed outputs spirals into degradation because it amplifies its own mistakes.

The paper derives phase transition curves: mathematically precise thresholds where the optimal strategy switches from keep-easy to keep-hard. These thresholds depend on dataset size, labeler quality, and picker quality. When these three align well, the switch happens early (small dataset wins). When alignment is poor, you never get the win because you cannot reliably tell hard from easy.

stages.s: Calculate phase transition threshold (dataset size breakpoint)
Choose strategy (keep-hard if high alignment, keep-easy if low)
Curated dataset with higher accuracy per training step, because each example is carefully chosen to maximize learning signal

math.words: Minimize one-over-n times (sum over i of p-i times loss-i plus regularization); where p-i is 1 if example-i is kept and 0 if pruned.
math.equation: min_w (1/n) * sum_i p_i * L(x_i^T * w; y_i) + (lambda/2) * ||w||^2
symbols: 1 if example i is kept, 0 if pruned by the oracle
the label (correct answer) for example i
the model weights (what we are training)
the loss for one example, here loss equals (z minus y) squared divided by 2
penalty strength (how much to penalize large weights to avoid overfitting)
total number of training examples (before pruning)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose we have 10 examples, alignment is high (labeler and picker both reliable), and we keep only the 5 hardest.
For the 5 kept examples with loss 0.2, 0.15, 0.25, 0.18, 0.22 and penalty term 0.5:
If we kept all 10 with 5 more examples of loss 0.05 each: (1/10) times (1.0 + 0.25) + 0.5 = 0.125 + 0.5 = 0.625
The curated set score 0.6 beats the full set score 0.625 because we eliminated easy examples that added noise.

math.note: The sum over kept examples (marked 1 in the list of binary flags, one per example) is divided by the original dataset size n, so the effective learning rate per kept example rises when you prune.

charts.title: Naive: use all data
rows: Accuracy on task A (after full training)
charts.note: Model trained on all 1.2M examples, including easy, noisy, and mislabeled ones. Overfits to noise and forgets old tasks.

charts.title: This paper: curated dataset
rows: Accuracy on task A (after curated training)
charts.note: Model trained on 100K curated examples (hard and correct). Stays focused because it avoids relearning easy examples. Retains knowledge across tasks and reaches higher accuracy faster, because it spends training budget on examples that move the needle.

items.html: If your pruner cannot reliably assess difficulty (e.g., it has access only to features, not labels), and your labeler is weak (noisy or biased), the phase transition threshold collapses. Curation becomes worthless. You keep examples you thought were hard but are actually mislabeled.

If alignment is low, keep-hard will make things worse by hoarding mislabeled hard examples. The paper predicts when keep-easy is optimal, but only if you compute alignment correctly. If you guess wrong, you amplify noise.

If your dataset is too small or alignment too poor, you never enter the regime where curated training beats full training. The curve shows when the win is possible; outside that region, you need all the data you have.

Before deciding to prune, compute rho and rho-star from your training set. These numbers tell you if you are in a regime where curation helps because they predict whether your labeler and picker are reliable. Only then commit to keep-hard or keep-easy.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a synthetic classifier on Gaussian-distributed data where you control the labeler quality and picker quality. Generate a training set of size n where each example is labeled correctly with probability rho (the alignment). Create a pruner that can identify difficulty via an oracle aligned with ground truth at rho-star. Train models with keep-hard, keep-easy, and keep-all strategies. Measure test accuracy at different dataset sizes and compare to the theory's phase transition prediction.
demo.metric_eq: Test accuracy = (correctly predicted on held-out set) / (total held-out examples); plot accuracy vs dataset size for each curation strategy and show where keep-hard crosses above keep-all.
demo.closing: The demo must show a clear crossover point where the curated strategy outperforms the full dataset, exactly where the paper's math predicts it should happen, because when alignment is high enough, concentrated signal beats dilute noise. This single plot makes the paradox visible: sometimes, deliberately throwing away data is the right move.
